note.question: How can a buyer assess intangible data before purchase when the seller is also a downstream competitor, and do free samples align with the seller's incentives?
note.overview: An incumbent data seller privately knows whether data have high or low value and makes a sample-volume, sale-volume, and price offer to an entrant buyer. In the main model, sale volume signals type without samples, free-sample volume signals type when samples are available, and price is a transfer rather than a signal. After the buyer accepts or rejects, the same firms play a Bayesian quantity-competition game using noisy demand forecasts. The paper characterizes separating and pooling equilibria and selects among them with lexicographically maximum sequential equilibrium.

components.label: Solution or estimation method
components.explanation: The authors solve the downstream Bayesian Cournot game from conditional expectations and then work backward to the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's type-dependent offer. Incentive compatibility identifies costly separating signals, and LMSE compares them with pooling. Comparative statics isolate data monetization and lost information advantage; extensions allow correlated forecast signals, a passive platform, and complementary products.

components.label: LMSE-refined signaling equilibrium followed by Bayesian quantity equilibrium
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is LMSE-refined signaling equilibrium followed by Bayesian quantity equilibrium. Backward induction first solves the retailers' simultaneous Bayesian quantity choices conditional on acquired data. In data trading, the buyer infers sigma from the seller's offer. Separating equilibria reveal type and achieve evaluation; pooling preserves the prior. The authors apply lexicographically maximum sequential equilibrium to select the high type's most profitable sustainable outcome and report that the separating equilibrium also survives the intuitive criterion whereas pooling does not.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: In the free-sample regime, the seller first chooses sample volume x_1; in both regimes it next chooses sale volume x or x_2 and data price p_d; the buyer then accepts or rejects. At the product-selling stage, demand variance sigma becomes common knowledge, data produce private noisy demand signals S_s and S_b, the two retailers simultaneously choose quantities q_s and q_b, and consumers purchase. Without samples the first sample stage is omitted. A high-value seller must distort its offer because a low-value seller gains both a higher price and retained information advantage by mimicking.
